intro: The finale of the “New World” Symphony opens with fast string figures and a theme in the brass. Before the end, melodies from all four movements return, and the final E major chord fades in the winds after the strings have stopped.

sections.label: A · String introduction and brass theme
sections.mNote: Rising string figures lead to the main theme in the brass.

sections.label: B · Clarinet theme in G major
sections.mNote: The clarinet plays the theme over quick figures in the cellos.

sections.label: Dev · Earlier tunes return
sections.mNote: Largo and scherzo themes return alongside the finale’s own melody.

sections.label: A′ · Main theme returns
sections.mNote: The opening theme leads a shortened return of earlier music.

sections.label: Coda · Largo chords return in the brass
sections.mNote: The slow movement’s chords return in the full orchestra.

sections.label: Link · Clarinets above a held bass
sections.mNote: The orchestra plays more softly beneath the winds.

sections.label: Close · E major, final wind chord
sections.mNote: The winds hold the final chord after the strings stop.

cues.title: Opening and main theme
cues.text: The strings begin alone and drive a short figure upwards. Winds and brass enter at the top of the climb. The brass then play the main theme, which has a broad opening phrase and a sharply accented reply.
cues.evidence: Šourek full score, movement IV, printed pp. 133–137, Allegro con fuoco. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ea/IMSLP717707-PMLP8710-00._DVORAK_-_SYMPHONY_NO._9,_OP._95_(BARTOS)_-_Conductor%27s_Score.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Second theme, solo clarinet
cues.text: A solo clarinet plays the second theme in G major. It holds long notes over quick figures in the cellos. The brass rests, and the flutes later join the clarinet.
cues.evidence: Šourek full score, printed pp. 146–148: solo clarinet, moving cellos and subsequent flute entries.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Completion of the score, 24 May 1893
cues.text: Dvořák finished the score at nine in the morning on 24 May 1893. That afternoon a telegram told him that his children had reached Southampton on their way to America, and he added the news beside the time of completion.
cues.evidence: Josef Kovařík’s memoir records the completion time and telegram annotation on 24 May 1893; reproduced at https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/.

cues.title: Themes from earlier movements
cues.text: The development combines themes from the second, third and fourth movements. The slow movement’s melody and the scherzo’s quick figures sound against the finale’s main theme. Dvořák changes their pairings and accompaniment, so that melodies from different movements occupy the same bars.
cues.evidence: The Dvořák work catalogue identifies the combination of themes from movements II, III and IV in the finale’s development: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/. Šourek full score, printed pp. 157–170.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recall of earlier movements
cues.text: In the finale of Beethoven’s Ninth, themes from the earlier movements are recalled at the start and then dropped. Dvořák brings them back in the development and adds more of them as the movement goes on. By the coda, every key idea of the symphony has returned.
cues.evidence: Dvořák work catalogue, Symphony No. 9, analysis of the fourth movement and the principle of reminiscence: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

cues.title: Public rehearsal, New York, 1893
cues.text: At the public rehearsal on 15 December 1893 the Herald asked musicians what the symphony meant for America. Seidl hoped it would lead younger composers towards “a truly national school”. Victor Herbert was asked whether it would shape the country’s music and replied: “Yes, if the composers are Dr. Dvořák.”
cues.evidence: New York Herald report of the full rehearsal, quoted in the première section of the Dvořák work catalogue: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

cues.title: Return of the main theme
cues.text: The finale’s main theme returns after the combination of earlier melodies. Its broad statement leads into a shortened recapitulation. Dvořák kept the longest treatment of material from the earlier movements for the expanded coda.
cues.evidence: The abbreviated recapitulation and expanded coda are described in the Dvořák work catalogue: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performances in Europe, 1894
cues.text: London heard the symphony first in Europe, on 21 June 1894. Czech audiences first heard it at Karlovy Vary on 20 July. In Prague, on 13 October, Dvořák conducted it himself at the National Theatre.
cues.evidence: Performance history in the Dvořák work catalogue, Symphony No. 9: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

cues.title: Title page, November 1893
cues.text: In November 1893 Anton Seidl asked for the score so that he could prepare its première. Shortly before Kovařík took it to him, Dvořák added From the New World to the title page. Until that evening the title page had read Symphony in E minor.
cues.evidence: Josef Kovařík’s memoir places the title-page addition in mid-November 1893, just before he delivered the score to Seidl; reproduced at https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/.

cues.title: Coda, return of the Largo chords
cues.text: The coda brings back themes from the earlier movements alongside the finale’s own. The chords that opened the Largo return, scored for full orchestra. The brass hold them in long notes while the strings rise against them.
cues.evidence: Šourek full score, coda, printed pp. 190–197; the Largo-chord reminiscence is identified in the Dvořák work catalogue.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Simrock, December 1893
cues.text: After the première Dvořák wrote to his publisher Simrock in Berlin that “the papers are saying that no composer has ever achieved a triumph such as this”. The applause was so long, he added, that he had to bow from his box “like a king (don’t laugh!)”.
cues.evidence: Dvořák to Fritz Simrock, December 1893, quoted in the première section of the Dvořák work catalogue: https://www.antonin-dvorak.cz/en/work/symphony-no-9/

cues.title: Clarinets over held bass, bar 310
cues.text: From bar 310 the orchestra makes a diminuendo after its large chords. The repeated string figures soften and the bass holds a long note. The clarinets enter above it with another quiet recollection before the final climb.
cues.evidence: Šourek full score, printed pp. 198–199, bars 310 onwards: diminuendo, held bass and clarinet soli.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final chord in E major
cues.text: The closing pages move towards E major. In the final bar the strings, trombones and timpani play their last chord short, while the woodwind, horns and trumpets hold theirs. The held chord makes a diminuendo to ppp under a long fermata.
cues.evidence: Šourek full score, printed pp. 200–204, particularly the final bar: short string, trombone and timpani notes against sustained wind, horn and trumpet notes, diminuendo to ppp and lunga corona.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Brass to solo clarinet
transitions.from: A · String introduction and brass theme
transitions.to: B · Clarinet theme in G major
transitions.how: The brass stop and the strings play more softly. A solo clarinet enters with the second theme in G major, in long phrases above quick figures in the cellos. The upper strings hold long chords beneath the melody.
transitions.evidence: Šourek full score, printed pp. 146–148, lyrical second subject.

transitions.title: From exposition into development
transitions.from: B · Clarinet theme in G major
transitions.how: The exposition’s closing figures diminish over a held bass. The first violins then play a rising phrase that begins the development. Above the moving strings, horns, trumpets and winds take up themes from the other movements.
transitions.evidence: Šourek full score, printed pp. 156–160: diminished closing figures, rising violin phrase and ensuing development.

transitions.title: Return of the main tune
transitions.how: Repeated wind chords and rising violin figures build towards the return of the main tune. Horns, bassoons and low strings give it weight below the high winds. The recapitulation is shorter than the exposition, and the largest build-up comes in the coda.
transitions.evidence: Šourek full score, printed pp. 170–172, rehearsal 8. The shorter recapitulation is described in the Dvořák work catalogue.

transitions.title: Tempo I into the coda
transitions.to: Coda · Largo chords return in the brass
transitions.how: At Tempo I, the quieter return is followed by long orchestral chords and a forceful line in bassoons, cellos and basses. The coda brings back earlier themes, including the Largo’s opening chord sequence. Brass sustains the harmony while the strings climb repeatedly beneath it.
transitions.evidence: Šourek full score, printed pp. 190–197, Tempo I and the coda; the Largo-chord return is identified in the Dvořák work catalogue.

transitions.title: Clarinets enter over the held bass
transitions.from: Coda · Largo chords return in the brass
transitions.to: Link · Clarinets above a held bass
transitions.how: The wind chords and repeated string figures diminish together. Cellos and basses stop their running notes and hold a quiet foundation. The clarinets begin a new phrase above it. The brass rests and the timpani roll fades.
transitions.evidence: Šourek full score, printed pp. 198–199, bars 310 onwards.

transitions.title: Into the final E major chord
transitions.from: Link · Clarinets above a held bass
transitions.to: Close · E major, final wind chord
transitions.how: The quiet wind recollection leads into the final orchestral build. The strings rise, and brass and timpani play emphatically as the music moves to E major. At the last chord the orchestra divides. Strings, trombones and timpani stop short, and winds, horns and trumpets hold the chord and diminish to ppp.
transitions.evidence: Šourek full score, printed pp. 200–204, concluding build and final chord.

source.title: Dvořák, Symphony No. 9, full score, critical edition edited by Otakar Šourek
source.locator: Movement IV, printed pp. 133–204: rising strings and the brass main tune, lyrical clarinet, returning themes and final E-major chord. Cymbals sound once, held across bars 64–66 on printed p. 146. There is no tuba part.

timeline.note: The strings begin alone, playing a short figure that rises towards the entry of the brass.
Horns and trumpets play the broad E-minor tune above moving strings.
A single soft cymbal stroke sounds across three bars before the clarinet melody.
The clarinet plays in G major above quick cello figures and held upper strings.
Themes from the Largo and scherzo pass through winds and brass above the moving strings.
The main tune returns across the orchestra before the quieter woodwind phrases.
Oboes and horns hand their phrases to clarinets, above quiet trombone chords, timpani and strings.
The clarinet plays the lyrical tune again, with the other winds and strings answering around it.
Flutes and strings broaden the song, then soften over quiet timpani and held chords.
Brass and timpani rejoin the winds and strings in the coda, which brings back the symphony’s earlier themes.
Clarinets play above a held bass; the horn call follows, with quiet timpani and trombone chords.
The orchestra moves towards E major; winds, horns and trumpets hold the final chord after the strings stop.

composer.epithet: Composer of the Slavonic Dances, who played viola in an opera orchestra for nine years before his music became widely known.
facts: Violist at Prague’s Provisional Theatre, 1862–71; organist and piano teacher
Prague Conservatory; director of New York’s National Conservatory, 1892–95
Nine symphonies; operas, concertos, chamber music, choral works and songs
composer.background:
In the village band at Nelahozeves, north of Prague, the musicians collected their money by stopping a couple halfway through a dance and asking them to pay. Young Antonín Dvořák handed his share straight to his father, the village butcher and innkeeper. “I belonged to ours as soon as I could fiddle a little,” he told the London Sunday Times on 10 May 1885. He was born in Nelahozeves on 8 September 1841.

At Zlonice, the schoolteacher Antonín Liehmann taught him harmony and several instruments. Dvořák remembered bringing home a polka for the band to try. The opening chord came out all right except for the cornet, whose part he had written in the wrong key. In 1857 he went to the Prague Organ School, graduating two years later. He played viola in a dance band which became the nucleus of the Provisional Theatre orchestra in 1862. For nine years he sat in the pit, often under Smetana, playing operas while writing his own music at home.
